Raw differences without that calibration need not estimate the corrected solution's error. Variable-step multistep methods also require updated coefficients and controlled history handling.

Two Runge-Kutta methods share a stage matrix and nodes but use different output weights. An order-p and order-q pair with q<p gives an output difference generally of order hq+1, estimating the lower-order defect. Shared stage evaluations reduce the cost. The adaptive step-size controller exponent must reflect this estimator order, rather than blindly the higher reported solution order.

Finite volume method OurBigBook.com
A scalar finite-volume update is monotone if increasing any input state cannot decrease any output state. A consistent conservative update preserves constants and has an invariant interval by comparison. On a periodic grid, or an infinite grid with summable perturbations, conservation and monotonicity imply L1 contraction of a monotone conservative scheme. Translation invariance then implies the total variation diminishing scheme property.

If S is the one-cell shift, TS=ST, and L1 contraction of a monotone conservative scheme applied to U,SU gives ∑j​∣(TU)j+1​−(TU)j​∣≤∑j​∣Uj+1​−Uj​∣. For f(u)=u2/2, linearization about a positive constant U gives an upwind finite difference scheme for advection equation: vjn+1​=(1−rU)vjn​+rUvj−1n​, where r=k/h. Words: 102 Articles: 1
Engquist-Osher method OurBigBook.com
The Engquist-Osher numerical flux is F(a,b)=f(0)+∫0a​max(f′(s),0)ds+∫0b​min(f′(s),0)ds. It sends positive-speed contributions from the left state and negative-speed contributions from the right state. Its consistency F(u,u)=f(u) and opposite monotonicities in the two arguments yield a monotone conservative scheme under the appropriate Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition. For the Inviscid Burgers equation, it is 21​max(a,0)2+21​min(b,0)2.

Words: 59
Engquist-Osher flux OurBigBook.com
For a flux that is a differentiable convex function with unique minimum at s∗​, define f+(u)=f(u)−f(s∗​) for u>s∗​ and zero otherwise, and f−(u)=f(u)−f(s∗​) for u<s∗​ and zero otherwise. The Engquist-Osher flux is F(a,b)=f(s∗​)+f+(a)+f−(b). Thus transsonic rarefaction wave states a≤s∗​≤b give F=f(s∗​), while reversed transsonic states give F=f(a)+f(b)−f(s∗​). This follows by integrating the positive and negative parts of f′.

Numerical flux (F(a,b))

Words: 150 Articles: 1
Finite volume method OurBigBook.com
A numerical flux approximates the transported quantity through a cell interface using nearby states. For a two-state flux F(a,b) approximating a scalar conservation law with flux f, consistency requires F(u,u)=f(u). A monotone conservative scheme uses a flux nondecreasing in its left state and nonincreasing in its right state, with a time step making the complete update monotone.

Godunov numerical flux (FG​(a,b))

Words: 97
Numerical flux OurBigBook.com
For a scalar conservation law whose flux is a convex function, the Godunov numerical flux is the physical flux at the origin of the entropy solution of the Riemann problem between states a,b. It is minu∈[a,b]​f(u) for a≤b and maxu∈[b,a]​f(u) for a>b. For a rarefaction wave, the characteristic speed is monotone across its states, so the origin sees either an endpoint or a zero-speed minimizing state. For a shock wave, its speed is (f(a)−f(b))/(a−b); the origin sees the left state if this speed is positive and the right state if negative, selecting the larger endpoint flux. Unlike the Godunov flux, the Engquist-Osher flux at reversed transsonic states may equal f(a)+f(b)−f(s∗​).

Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
For a continuous increasing scalar function, retain an interval whose endpoints bracket a target value, evaluate its midpoint, and keep the half that still brackets the target. Each step halves the interval length. Applied to a strictly increasing water-level equation, this finds its unique solution to any specified error tolerance.

Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
An implicit time-stepping method determines a new solution value through an equation involving that same value. A small-step contraction mapping argument often establishes local solvability when the vector field is Lipschitz continuous. Examples include the Backward Euler method, implicit Runge-Kutta methods and implicit linear multistep methods. Solvability of the update is a separate issue from stability of a numerical method.

Words: 435 Articles: 6
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
A multigrid method combines relaxation of high-frequency fine-grid errors with coarse-grid correction of smooth errors. Residual restriction, an approximate coarse error solve, error prolongation and post-smoothing form a two-grid cycle; recursive coarse solves give multilevel cycles.

Full multigrid

Words: 79
Multigrid method OurBigBook.com
Full multigrid solves first on a coarse mesh, interpolates that approximation to the next finer mesh, and applies a fixed number of geometric multigrid V-cycles before proceeding to the next level. If interpolation introduces only the expected discretization-scale error and the cycle count reduces the inherited error sufficiently at every level, the final algebraic error matches the fine-grid discretization error. The geometric sum of level costs is then O(N), unlike reducing an arbitrary fine-grid initial error by an arbitrarily small tolerance.

Multigrid method OurBigBook.com
For the one-dimensional Poisson equation, use linear interpolation, full-weighting restriction, an exact coarse solve, and one pre- and one post-sweep of weighted Jacobi with weight 2/3. On a pair of harmonics θ,θ+π, put s=sin2(θ/2) and c=1−s. The coarse correction is C=(s−s​−cc​), and the smoother is S=diag(1−4s/3,1−4c/3). The rank-one error operator SCS has nonzero eigenvalue s(1−4s/3)2+c(1−4c/3)2=1/9. This exact harmonic calculation illustrates mesh-independent two-grid contraction for the constant-coefficient model; it is not an unconditional result for arbitrary operators or transfer choices.

Words: 77
Multigrid method OurBigBook.com
A geometric multigrid V-cycle pre-smooths an approximate solution, restricts its residual, recursively solves the coarse error equation once from zero, prolongs and adds that error correction, and post-smooths. The recursion ends in a direct solve on a small coarsest grid. With fixed sweep counts and bounded stencil work, coarsening in d dimensions gives total work O(N)∑j≥0​2−dj=O(N) per cycle. A mesh-independent convergence factor also requires compatible coarse approximation and effective smoothing; linear work alone does not prove convergence.

Full-weighting restriction transfers a fine-grid residual to a coarser grid by local averaging. In one dimension its weights are (1,2,1)/4; in two dimensions they are the tensor-product stencil (121​242​121​)/16. For linear or bilinear interpolation P and coarsening by two in every direction, it equals 2−dPT in unweighted coordinates. This scaling makes restriction the adjoint of interpolation for mesh-weighted inner products.

Finite element method OurBigBook.com
On a shape-regular mesh in dimensions at most three, nodal piecewise-linear interpolation of u∈H2(Ω) satisfies
∥u−Ih​u∥L2(Ω)​+h∥u−Ih​u∥H1(Ω)​≤Ch2∥u∥H2(Ω)​,
(8)
where h is the largest element diameter and C is independent of h. For homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, Ih​u belongs to the conforming finite element space. Scaling each element to a reference element gives the estimate; shape regularity bounds the scaling constants, while subtraction of an affine function leaves an error controlled by the second derivatives.

The mass matrix is the Gram matrix of a finite element basis in the L2 inner product. Its coefficient quadratic form is the squared L2 norm of the represented trial function, so it is a positive-definite matrix for a linearly independent basis.

A mass eigenstate diagonalizes the Hermitian mass operator or mass matrix and has a definite mass. In a flavor basis with off-diagonal mass terms, it is a linear combination of flavor states. For unstable particles, decay propagation instead involves an effective complex matrix; its eigenvectors need not inherit the orthogonality of a Hermitian mass problem.

On a one-dimensional uniform finite element mesh of spacing h, let w be an affine function and ϕi​ the interior piecewise-linear hat functions. The weighted mass matrix has entries
Wii​=32h​w(xi​),Wi,i+1​=Wi+1,i​=12h​(w(xi​)+w(xi+1​)),
(9)
and zero entries for nonadjacent indices. The diagonal product ϕi2​ is symmetric about xi​ and integrates to 2h/3; the neighbouring product is symmetric about (xi​+xi+1​)/2 and integrates to h/6. The odd part of an affine function integrates to zero around each centre, giving the formulas. This evaluates a variable reaction term exactly without substituting a constant coefficient or a quadrature approximation.

Céa's lemma

Words: 141 Articles: 1
Galerkin orthogonality OurBigBook.com
For a continuous coercive bilinear form with continuity constant M and coercivity constant α, a conforming finite-element solution satisfies
∥u−uh​∥V​≤αM​infvh​∈Vh​​∥u−vh​∥V​.

For a symmetric problem measured in its energy norm, the constant is one.
For any vh​∈Vh​, Galerkin orthogonality gives a(e,e)=a(e,u−vh​), where e=u−uh​. Coercivity and continuity yield α∥e∥V2​≤M∥e∥V​∥u−vh​∥V​. Divide by ∥e∥V​ when it is nonzero and take the infimum. In the symmetric case, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in the energy norm gives the constant one.

Complex quadratic Schur criterion (∣ab−cb∣≤∣a∣2−∣c∣2)

Words: 167
Schur stability criterion OurBigBook.com
For a complex polynomial p(z)=az2+bz+c, assume ∣a∣>∣c∣ and put D=∣a∣2−∣c∣2 and E=ab−cb. Both roots of a polynomial lie in the closed unit disk if and only if ∣E∣≤D. Strict inequality puts both roots in the open disk. Under the strict product assumption ∣c/a∣<1, any unit-modulus root is automatically simple.
To prove the strict version, define p#(z)=z2p(1/z)​ and q=ap−cp#=z(Dz+E). On the unit circle ∣p#∣=∣p∣, so the Rouche theorem shows that a stable p and q have the same two interior zeros. Conversely Dp=aq+cq#, and the same Rouche theorem implies that two interior zeros of q give two interior zeros of p. The nonzero root of q is −E/D, proving the criterion. The closed version follows by continuity, replacing b by (1−ε)b in the sufficiency direction. In the necessity direction with a boundary root, replace p(z) by p(z/r) for r<1 close to one and let r→1. The product of the two roots of a polynomial excludes two unit-modulus roots and excludes a repeated unit-modulus root.

Words: 133

For Hermitian matrices H1​,…,Hm​ and t≥0, let S(t)=∏j=1m​e−itHj​. Then

Differentiating e−iuABeiuA and integrating yields ∥[e−isA,B]∥≤s∥[A,B]∥, because unitary operators preserve the norm. Integrating s from zero to t gives t2∥[A,B]∥/2. Inductively separate H1​ from the remaining sum, use the triangle inequality on their commutator, and apply the telescoping bound for products of operators to obtain the displayed many-term bound.
Repeating steps of size t/k and telescoping across k steps gives

An interpolation polynomial for distinct nodes x0​,…,xn​ and prescribed values y0​,…,yn​ is a polynomial p satisfying p(xi​)=yi​. There is a unique such polynomial of degree at most n: the Lagrange interpolation polynomial constructs it explicitly, and uniqueness follows because a nonzero degree-at-most-n difference cannot have n+1 distinct roots. Newton interpolation polynomials express the same object using divided differences.

Interpolation nodes from best uniform approximation (ℓn​(f)=pn∗​)

Words: 84
Polynomial interpolation OurBigBook.com
For a real continuous function on a compact interval, choose its best uniform approximation pn∗​ of polynomial degree at most n. If its error is nonzero, the Chebyshev alternation theorem supplies n+2 ordered alternating extrema. The intermediate value theorem gives a zero of f−pn∗​ in each intervening interval. At these n+1 distinct points, the polynomial interpolant is exactly pn∗​. If the best error is zero, arbitrary distinct nodes suffice. The Weierstrass approximation theorem shows that these function-dependent interpolants converge uniformly. The nodes depend on the target function; the conclusion does not provide one universal node sequence for every continuous target.

The leading coefficient of rj​ has sign (−1)n+2−j, so all summands in the leading coefficient of r have the same nonzero sign. There is a unique λ canceling degree n+1 in t−λr. Increasing order matters: for the permutation (0,1/3,1,2/3) the alternating interpolant is already the quadratic −1+9x(1−x), so the leading-coefficient assertion for n=2 fails.

Lagrange cardinal polynomial OurBigBook.com

For 1≤k≤n, its numerator's kth derivative at one is k! times a sum of products of n−k nonnegative factors 1−tj​. At most one factor vanishes, and at least one product avoids it, so that sum is strictly positive. The same alternating nodal signs therefore maximize every endpoint derivative simultaneously.

Orthogonality kills the quotient when a degree-2n−1 polynomial is divided by Tn​; its remainder is recovered by interpolation. At each step of Gaussian elimination, select the largest absolute entry in the uneliminated part of the current column and interchange rows to put it on the diagonal. A nonsingular trailing Schur complement has a nonzero entry in its first column, so this procedure always finds a nonzero pivot in exact arithmetic. The permutation matrix P records row interchanges; earlier multipliers must be interchanged too when assembling the lower-triangular factor. This yields the LU decomposition PA=LU with unit diagonal in L. Searching within columns and interchanging rows is distinct from interchanging columns.

Row echelon form

Words: 96
Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
A matrix is in row echelon form if zero rows follow all nonzero rows, each nonzero row has a first nonzero entry (pivot) to the right of the pivot in the preceding row, and entries below each pivot vanish. Elementary row operations bring every matrix to this form: choose a nonzero entry in the earliest nonzero column, swap its row to the top, eliminate entries below it, and continue on the remaining submatrix. The nonzero rows are independent by their successively positioned pivots; the pivot columns are independent and span the column space. Thus the number of pivots equals both row rank and column rank.

Elementary row operation

Words: 125 Articles: 1
Gaussian elimination OurBigBook.com
An elementary row operation interchanges two rows of a matrix, multiplies one row by a nonzero scalar, or adds a scalar multiple of another row to it. These invertible operations are used in Gaussian elimination. For a square matrix, interchange changes the sign of its determinant, multiplication scales its determinant by the same scalar, and adding another row leaves its determinant unchanged, by multilinearity and alternation.
Elementary matrix
Words: 65
Elementary row operation OurBigBook.com
An elementary matrix is obtained by applying one elementary row operation to the identity matrix. Multiplying A by it on the left performs the same row operation on A. Such a matrix is invertible: reverse a row swap, reverse a nonzero row scaling by its reciprocal, or reverse adding a multiple of another row by adding its negative. Right multiplication gives an elementary column operation. In particular these operations preserve matrix rank.

The strict decay convention for a linear stability domain demands that every numerical mode tends to zero on the Dahlquist test equation. For a one-step stability function it requires ∣R(z)∣<1; for a multistep method it requires every amplification root to have modulus below one. This differs from a boundedness convention that allows simple unit-circle roots, and from mesh-uniform finite-time numerical stability. Cambridge numerical analysis notes use the decay convention. Explicitly specifying the convention is essential for methods with undamped modes.

For even s, the node polynomial ∏j=0s​(t−j) is odd about s/2, so its integral vanishes and exactness extends through degree s+1. The weights need not remain positive as the number of nodes increases.

Simpson's rule (∫aa+2h​f≈3h​[f(a)+4f(a+h)+f(a+2h)])

Words: 91
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
Simpson's rule integrates the quadratic interpolant through two endpoints and their midpoint. It is exact also on cubic polynomials. On [0,2], define the raw kernel K(t)=L[(x−t)+3​], where L is integral minus the rule. Then K(t)=−t3(4−3t)/12 for 0≤t≤1 and K(t)=−(2−t)3(3t−2)/12 for 1≤t≤2. It is strictly negative inside the interval and integrates to −1/15. The Peano kernel theorem therefore gives the sharp bound ∣L(f)∣≤∥f(4)∥∞​/90; f(x)=x4/24 attains equality. Scaling to endpoint spacing h gives h5/90. The normalized Peano kernel is K/3!, so the external factorial must be omitted when using that normalization.

Convergence of positive quadrature on continuous functions

Words: 32
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
On a compact interval, positive quadrature rule weights whose sum is the interval length define uniformly bounded functionals on continuous functions. If the rules eventually integrate every fixed polynomial exactly, the Weierstrass approximation theorem proves convergence for every continuous function.

Nodal-polynomial criterion for quadrature exactness

Words: 30
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
An (n+1)-node quadrature rule already exact through degree n is exact through degree n+1+k exactly when its nodal polynomial
Qn+1​(x)=∏i=0n​(x−xi​)
(105)
is orthogonal to every polynomial of degree at most k.

Degree ceiling for quadrature exactness

Words: 32
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
No (n+1)-node quadrature rule for a positive interval weight can be exact through degree 2n+2, because it evaluates the nonnegative nodal square Qn+12​ as zero although its integral is positive.

Positivity of quadrature weights from degree 2n exactness

Words: 39
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
If an (n+1)-node quadrature rule for a positive interval weight is exact through degree 2n, every weight is positive. Indeed, applying the rule to the square of the corresponding degree-n Lagrange cardinal polynomial isolates that weight.

Convergence of positive quadrature rules

Words: 41
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
If each (n+1)-node quadrature rule is exact through degree n and has positive weights, then it converges on every continuous function. The Weierstrass approximation theorem reduces the error to the uniform polynomial-approximation error, while exactness on constants controls the sum of the weights.

Moment matching

Words: 22
Quadrature rule OurBigBook.com
A quadrature rule is exact through degree d precisely when its node weights reproduce the first d+1 moments of the integration measure.

Midpoint method

Words: 34
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
The midpoint method advances an ordinary differential equation using a derivative evaluated at a temporal midpoint. Its explicit form predicts that midpoint from the initial derivative, while the implicit midpoint rule solves for the derivative at the mean of the endpoint states.

Collocation method

Words: 31
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
A collocation method chooses an approximate solution from a finite-dimensional trial space and forces the residual of a differential equation to vanish at selected nodes. Collocation Runge-Kutta methods apply this principle to polynomial approximations on each time step.

QR algorithm

Words: 23
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
The QR algorithm computes eigenvalues through repeated QR decompositions and similarity updates. Shifted and unshifted forms have different convergence rates; the unshifted QR algorithm uses a zero shift at every step.

Iterative method

Words: 31
Numerical analysis OurBigBook.com
An iterative method approximates a solution by repeatedly updating an initial guess. In numerical linear algebra, a stationary iterative method for a linear system uses a fixed iteration map; other iterations can change their update rule or search space at each step.
